quizzes.title: The Finance Commission at a Glance
quizzes.passage:
The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023. It is a constitutional body, which means that its role is laid down in the Constitution itself. Its basic task is to recommend how tax revenues are distributed between the Central Government and the State Governments. Because the sharing of tax revenue lies at the heart of India's federal arrangement, the Commission's work has a direct bearing on the finances of every State.

The Commission works as one body made up of a Chairperson and other members. Each member holds office for a specified tenure. The Commission is constituted at intervals, so it is not a permanent body that works without a break. The 16th Commission is part of a series of such bodies that have been set up since 1951.

The Government has accepted the key recommendations of the Commission for the 2026-31 period. This means that the report now shapes the transfer of resources between the Union and the States during those years. Apart from the division of taxes, the Commission also makes recommendations on grants, so its role covers more than tax sharing alone. The report is a formal document that sets out the Commission's recommendations for the period it covers, and the Commission's work is tied to that period from start to finish.

questions.q: Who tabled the 16th Finance Commission Report in the Lok Sabha?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Union Finance Minister tabled the report in Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Generally, for how long are the members of the Finance Commission appointed?
questions.explanation: The booklet says members are appointed by the President for a specified tenure, generally 5 years.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Central Government must accept every suggestion made by the Finance Commission.
Reason (R): The Central Government is not bound by Finance Commission suggestions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The booklet states the Centre is not bound by Finance Commission suggestions, so A is false and R is true.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Article 280   ->   B. Constitutional body that recommends tax revenue distribution
II. Article 281   ->   D. Report with Action Taken Memorandum laid before Parliament
III. Composition of the Commission   ->   C. One Chairperson and four other members
IV. Chairperson of the 16th Commission   ->   A. Dr. Arvind Panagariya
questions.explanation: Article 280 matches the constitutional body, Article 281 matches the laid report, the composition matches C, and the Chairperson matches A.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the 16th Finance Commission:
I. Its Chairperson is Dr. Arvind Panagariya.
II. The President of India constitutes the Commission every five years and never earlier.
III. Its members are appointed by the President of India.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement II is false because the Commission is constituted every five years or earlier if required, so only I and III are correct.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the 16th Finance Commission are correct?
I. The Commission was set up under Article 280 of the Constitution.
II. It recommends the distribution of tax revenues between the Centre and the States.
III. Its recommendations bind the Central Government.
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while statement III is false since the Centre is not bound by Finance Commission suggestions.

questions.q: Dr. Arvind Panagariya, the Chairperson of the 16th Finance Commission, is a former Vice-Chairman of which body?
questions.explanation: The booklet describes Dr. Arvind Panagariya as a former Vice-Chairman of NITI Aayog.

quizzes.title: Set Up, Members and Reports
quizzes.passage:
The 16th Finance Commission was set up in 2023 to recommend how tax revenue is distributed between the Centre and the States. It is a constitutional body, so its role has a formal place in India's federal structure. The Commission consists of a Chairperson and other members, and each member serves for a specified tenure rather than on an open-ended basis.

The President of India constitutes each Finance Commission at intervals, and the recommendations of the 16th Commission cover the period from 2026 to 2031. The Government has accepted the key recommendations for that period.

The report of the Commission is a formal document. It reaches Parliament together with an Action Taken Memorandum, which records the steps the Government has taken on the recommendations. The 16th Commission is part of a long series of Finance Commissions, the first of which was appointed in 1951.

quizzes.title: Grants, Cess and Surcharge
quizzes.passage:
The Constitution provides for grants-in-aid from central resources to the States, so the Union can support State finances beyond the sharing of tax revenue. Grants of this kind come in two broad types, and the two types differ in how they are made and in the purposes they serve. Grants are an important part of the financial relationship between the Union and the States.

Some grants are given to States on the basis of the Finance Commission's recommendations, and they are meant for States that need financial help. Others are made by the Centre for purposes it chooses, and these may be given for any public purpose.

Apart from grants, the Centre also collects levies such as the cess and the surcharge. A cess is a levy imposed for a specific purpose, and a surcharge is an extra amount added to the base tax of some taxpayers. The Centre also runs a scheme that provides long-term loans to States.

questions.q: Which type of grant is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India every year?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that statutory grants under Article 275 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India every year.

questions.q: Under which kind of grant does the Centre have no obligation to make payments?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Centre is under no obligation to give discretionary grants, which lie within its discretion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cess is part of the divisible pool and is shared with the States.
Reason (R): Cesses are excluded from the divisible pool and are not shared with State Governments.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Cesses are excluded from the divisible pool and not shared with States, so A is false and R is true.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Surcharge   ->   B. Additional tax on high-income earners
II. SASCI   ->   C. Long-term interest-free loans for capital projects
III. Article 282   ->   A. Discretionary grants for any public purpose
IV. Article 275   ->   D. Statutory grants to States in need
questions.explanation: The surcharge matches the high-income tax, SASCI matches the interest-free loans, Article 282 matches discretionary grants, and Article 275 matches statutory grants.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about grants and levies:
I. Statutory grants under Article 275 are given to every State in the country.
II. Cess is mandatory for all taxpayers, including individuals, companies and firms.
III. The Centre is under an obligation to give discretionary grants under Article 282.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement II is correct, since statutory grants are not given to every State and the Centre has no obligation for discretionary grants.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about grants and levies are correct?
I. The surcharge is shared with State Governments through the divisible pool.
II. SASCI provides long-term, interest-free loans to State Governments.
III. Discretionary grants are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India every year.
questions.explanation: Only statement II is correct, since the surcharge is not shared with States and charged grants are statutory, not discretionary.

questions.q: Which levy is not shared with State Governments and is at the exclusive disposal of the Union Government?
questions.explanation: The booklet states the surcharge is not shared with State Governments and is at the exclusive disposal of the Union Government.

quizzes.title: Grants, Levies and Loans
quizzes.passage:
Grants-in-aid are one way in which the Union supports the finances of State Governments. The Constitution allows Parliament to make grants to States that need financial assistance, and such grants are not extended to every State. Another category of grants is made by the Centre for any public purpose, and the Centre decides whether to make such grants at all.

Levies are a separate matter. The Centre can impose a cess for a specific purpose, and the money raised must be used for that purpose. A surcharge is an additional tax on top of the base tax, aimed at people with high incomes.

The Centre also runs a scheme that gives States long-term loans for capital projects. The loans support lasting assets that the States create, and they are given over a long repayment period.

questions.explanation: The booklet states statutory grants are made under Article 275.

questions.q: What is the nature of SASCI loans with respect to interest? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet says SASCI provides long-term, interest-free loans to State Governments.

quizzes.title: Impact, Concerns and the Commissions
quizzes.passage:
Finance Commissions have been a regular feature of India's fiscal federalism since 1951, and each one makes recommendations on how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the States. The sharing takes place through a divisible pool, and the share given to States from that pool is among the most debated figures in public finance.

The debate has several strands. Some have argued that the share is too low for States' needs, and that States have sought a higher share. Others focus on the formula that splits the States' share among the States, since the weights given to different criteria change the amount each State receives.

The concerns about the formula relate to income, demography and economic performance, and to the effect of those factors on particular regions. Some States point to the features that make them distinct, while others want the formula to reward performance more directly.

questions.q: What percentage share of the divisible pool did States demand, which the 16th Finance Commission report did not adopt?
questions.explanation: The booklet notes that the States' share stays at 41 per cent despite demands for 50 per cent.

questions.q: The retained 41 per cent vertical share is said to give States which benefit?
questions.explanation: The booklet says retaining the 41 per cent share enhances revenue predictability for States.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Discontinuing revenue-deficit grants could adversely affect Hill and Special-category States.
Reason (R): Hill and Special-category States face structural and geographic fiscal disadvantages.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are in the booklet, and the structural disadvantages are the reason the discontinued grants would hurt these States.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while statement III is false because K.C. Neogy chaired the First Commission.

quizzes.title: Shares, Chairpersons and Concerns
quizzes.passage:
Finance Commissions have been appointed periodically for several decades, and each one makes recommendations on how the Centre's tax revenue should be shared with the States. The sharing is done through a divisible pool, and the share allotted to States from that pool is one of the most debated figures in Indian public finance.

In the 16th Commission's report, the share of the divisible pool given to States has been kept at the existing level, and the Commission has said this will give States greater predictability in their revenue. Some observers have said the level is too low, and that States had sought a larger share from the pool.

The Commission has also revised the formula that decides how the States' share is split among States. The revised criteria are said to protect fiscally weaker States. The report has also drawn concern about the weight given to certain criteria, including the demographic factor, and about the discontinuation of certain grants.
